questions.q: Which best describes a business logic vulnerability?
choices: A memory-corruption bug in a third-party library used by the application
A flaw in the design and implementation of an application that lets an attacker elicit unintended behavior, often by manipulating legitimate functionality
A weakness in a cryptographic primitive that allows ciphertext to be decrypted without the key
A server misconfiguration such as leaving default credentials enabled
questions.explain: Logic flaws are flaws in an application's design and implementation that let an attacker elicit unintended behavior and potentially turn legitimate functionality toward a malicious goal. They usually come from failing to anticipate unusual application states and handle them safely.

questions.q: Which other names are used for business logic vulnerabilities?
choices: Application logic vulnerabilities
Logic flaws
Injection flaws
Side-channel vulnerabilities
questions.explain: "Business logic" just means the set of rules that define how the application operates. Those rules aren't always related to a business, so the flaws are also called application logic vulnerabilities or simply logic flaws.

questions.q: True or false: In "business logic vulnerability", the word "business" means these flaws can only occur in applications that handle commercial transactions.
questions.explain: "Business logic" refers to the rules that define how any application operates, whether or not they relate to a business.

questions.q: True or false: Automated vulnerability scanners are generally effective at finding logic flaws, because logic flaws follow a small number of generic patterns.
questions.explain: Logic flaws are extremely diverse and often unique to an application. Finding them usually takes human knowledge, such as understanding the business domain or what an attacker might want, which makes them hard for scanners to detect and a good target for manual testers and bug bounty hunters.

questions.q: Why are logic flaws often invisible to people who aren't explicitly looking for them?
choices: They only occur in client-side JavaScript, which testers rarely read
They are always hidden behind authentication
Normal use of the application typically won't expose them
They exist only in compiled native code, not in web applications
questions.explain: Ordinary users following the expected flow won't trigger them. An attacker finds them by interacting with the application in ways the developers never intended.

questions.q: Developers assume users will only send data through a web browser. What is the likely consequence?
choices: The server rejects any request that wasn't sent from a browser
The application becomes tamper-proof, because browsers enforce form constraints
All input validation is moved to the server
The application relies on weak client-side controls to validate input, which an attacker can bypass with an intercepting proxy
questions.explain: Flawed assumptions about how users interact with the application lead to inadequate validation. If developers assume browser-only input, validation may live entirely in client-side controls, and an intercepting proxy gets around those easily.

questions.q: Under which conditions are logic flaws especially likely to creep into an application?
choices: In small applications written by a single developer who understands all of the code
In overly complicated systems where developers working on one component make undocumented assumptions about how other components work
In applications that document every assumption made at each stage
Only in applications that have no authentication
questions.explain: Logic flaws are common in overly complicated systems that even the development team doesn't fully understand. A developer on one component may make flawed assumptions about another component, and if those assumptions aren't documented, flaws creep in easily.

questions.q: What fundamentally determines the impact of a given logic flaw?
choices: The programming language the application is written in
Whether an automated scanner found the flaw
The functionality the flaw is related to
The number of users the application has
questions.explain: Impact varies widely. A flaw in authentication can seriously damage overall security, and a flaw in financial transactions can cause large losses through stolen funds and fraud.

questions.q: A logic flaw exists in an application's authentication mechanism. Which outcomes could it lead to?
choices: Privilege escalation
Bypassing authentication entirely
Access to sensitive data and functionality
A larger attack surface for other exploits
Nothing serious, because logic flaws are always low-impact
questions.explain: Authentication logic flaws can allow privilege escalation or a full authentication bypass, giving access to sensitive data and functionality and exposing more attack surface. Logic flaws are not inherently low-impact. Any unintended behavior can potentially lead to high-severity attacks.

questions.q: True or false: Quirky logic that you can't work out how to exploit yourself can safely be left unfixed.
questions.explain: Quirky logic should ideally be fixed even if you can't find an exploit, because someone else may be able to.

questions.q: True or false: A logic flaw that gives an attacker no direct benefit can still be a problem.
questions.explain: Even when attackers can't profit directly, a logic flaw may still let a malicious party damage the business in some way.

questions.q: Which of the following are key ways to prevent business logic vulnerabilities?
choices: Make sure developers and testers understand the domain the application serves
Avoid implicit assumptions about user behavior or about the behavior of other parts of the application
Rely on client-side validation to stop nonsensical values from reaching the server
Depend on automated scanners to catch logic flaws before release
questions.explain: The two keys are domain understanding and not making implicit assumptions. Client-side validation is easily bypassed, and scanners are poor at finding logic flaws.

questions.q: Which development practices help a team spot logic flaws early?
choices: Maintain clear design documents and data flows for all transactions and workflows, noting the assumptions made at each stage
Write code as clearly as possible, and document unavoidably complex cases
Note references to other code that uses each component, and consider side-effects if a malicious party manipulated those dependencies
Keep assumptions undocumented so attackers can't learn them
Divide knowledge of the components so that no developer needs to understand the application as a whole
questions.explain: Documenting assumptions, writing clear code, and tracking dependencies with their possible side-effects all help developers and testers understand the expected behavior. Undocumented assumptions and fragmented understanding are exactly how logic flaws get in.

questions.q: After a logic flaw has been found and fixed, what is the recommended next step?
choices: Treat it as a one-time human error and move on, since logic flaws are unique
Add a client-side check that blocks the input that triggered it
Add the specific payload to an automated scanner's signature list
Analyze why the flaw existed and how the team missed it, to find weaknesses in the development process
questions.explain: Logic flaws often come from bad practices early in development. Finding the root cause, and why it was missed, lets small process changes stop similar flaws at the source or catch them earlier.

questions.q: What should you do with the assumptions you have made about server-side state?
choices: Enforce them in client-side JavaScript so invalid state never reaches the server
Identify them and implement logic that verifies they hold, including checking that each input value is sensible before proceeding
Assume they hold once the user has authenticated
Encrypt them so users can't read them
questions.explain: Prevention means making assumptions explicit and verifying them on the server, for example by checking that every input value is sensible before acting on it.

questions.q: Why are client-side validation controls ineffective as a security measure?
choices: Browsers routinely disable JavaScript validation to improve performance
Client-side validation only runs on GET requests
An attacker can use an intercepting proxy such as Burp Proxy to change data after the browser sends it but before the server-side logic receives it
Client-side code is unable to check numeric ranges
questions.explain: Tampering with requests in transit makes client-side controls useless. Without integrity checks and server-side validation, the server is accepting attacker-controlled data at face value.

questions.q: A bank's transfer handler takes `$transferAmount` straight from `$_POST['amount']` and completes the transfer if `$transferAmount <= $currentBalance`. Otherwise it blocks the transfer. An attacker submits amount = -1000 for a transfer to a victim. What is the likely result?
choices: The check passes because -1000 is less than the balance, and the money moves the wrong way: the attacker receives $1000 from the victim
The check fails because a negative amount is treated as exceeding the balance
The transfer is blocked because POST parameters cannot hold negative numbers
The attacker's balance goes down by $1000 as with a normal transfer
questions.explain: Nothing rejects negative values. -1000 always compares as less than the current balance, so the transfer is approved, and sending -$1000 may result in the attacker receiving $1000 from the victim.

questions.q: True or false: With the check `if ($transferAmount <= $currentBalance)`, a user whose balance is $0 is blocked from submitting a transfer of -500.
questions.explain: -500 <= 0 is true, so the check approves it. The check only compares against the balance and never ensures the amount is positive.

questions.q: Why are simple flaws like the negative-transfer bug easy to miss in development and testing?
choices: They only appear under heavy load
The web interface's client-side controls may block such inputs, so testing through the UI never sends them to the server-side logic
Server logs never record negative values
They only affect applications written in PHP
questions.explain: If the browser form rejects negative numbers, testers using the UI never see the server accept them. An attacker sending requests directly does.

questions.q: When auditing an application for flaws in handling unconventional input, which kinds of input should you try?
choices: Exceptionally high numeric values
Exceptionally low numeric values
Abnormally long strings in text fields
Unexpected data types
Only values in the ranges legitimate users typically enter
questions.explain: The point is to try input in ranges that legitimate users are unlikely to ever enter, using tools such as Burp Proxy and Repeater, and then see how the application responds.

questions.q: While submitting unconventional values, which questions should you try to answer from the application's responses?
choices: Are any limits imposed on the data?
What happens when you reach those limits?
Is any transformation or normalization being performed on your input?
Would a typical legitimate user ever enter this value?
questions.explain: Limits, behavior at those limits, and transformation or normalization of input can all expose weak validation. Whether a normal user would enter the value doesn't matter, because the target is values legitimate users are unlikely to enter.

questions.q: True or false: If one form on a website fails to safely handle unconventional input, other forms on the same site are likely to have the same problem.
questions.explain: Weak input handling tends to be systematic. One vulnerable form suggests others share the same issue.

questions.q: An application applies strict checks when a user first registers but enforces the same rules loosely afterward. Which flawed assumption does this reflect?
choices: That users will always supply mandatory input
That users will always follow the intended sequence of steps
That a user and their data, having passed strict controls once, can be trusted indefinitely
That testers are familiar with the application's domain
questions.explain: Trusted users won't always remain trustworthy. If business rules and security measures aren't applied consistently throughout the application, the result is loopholes an attacker can exploit.

questions.q: Why can removing a parameter be especially effective when multiple functions are implemented in the same server-side script?
choices: Removing parameters makes the server skip authentication for the request
Smaller requests get past web application firewall size limits
Browsers can't send requests with missing parameters, so the server never handles that case
Whether a parameter is present may decide which code runs, so removing it can reach code paths that are supposed to be out of reach
questions.explain: Browsers may enforce required fields, but attackers can remove parameters in transit. When a parameter's presence or absence selects the code path, removing it can expose functionality that was never meant to be reachable.

questions.q: When probing for logic flaws by removing parameters, which practices are recommended?
choices: Remove only one parameter at a time
Try deleting the parameter name as well as its value
Follow multi-stage processes through to completion
Remove all parameters at once to cover the most code paths in a single request
Test only URL and POST parameters, since cookies don't affect code paths
questions.explain: Removing one parameter at a time ensures all relevant code paths are reached. Deleting the name and deleting the value are usually handled differently. Tampering in one step can affect a later step, so follow the process to the end. Cookies should be checked as well as URL and POST parameters.

questions.q: True or false: Servers typically handle a parameter sent with an empty value the same way as a parameter that has been removed entirely.
questions.explain: The server will typically handle the two cases differently, which is why you should try deleting the parameter name as well as the value.

questions.q: A site has users log in on one page and then enter a two-factor code on a separate page, but it never checks that the second step was completed. What can an attacker with valid credentials do?
choices: Nothing, because the login page itself enforces 2FA
Skip the verification page and access the account, bypassing 2FA entirely
Only read the 2FA code, not use it
Change the victim's password without logging in
questions.explain: The site assumes users always complete the workflow and never verifies that they did. An attacker can therefore skip the verification step altogether.

questions.q: What is the name of the technique where you directly request pages or endpoints in an order the interface doesn't offer, such as skipping steps of a workflow?
questions.explain: After seeing a request, an attacker can replay it at will (e.g. with Burp Proxy and Repeater) and use forced browsing to interact with the server in any order, leaving the application in an unexpected state.

questions.q: Which of these are ways to test a multi-step workflow for sequence-related logic flaws?
choices: Skip certain steps
Access a single step more than once
Return to earlier steps
Submit different sets of parameters to the same URL to reach different steps
Complete the steps only in the order the interface guides you
questions.explain: Submit requests in an unintended sequence and pay attention to how each step is reached. Sometimes steps are distinguished by parameter sets sent to one URL rather than by different URLs.

questions.q: Submitting workflow requests out of sequence often causes exceptions because expected variables are null or uninitialized. How should you treat the resulting error messages and debug output?
choices: Ignore them as noise unrelated to the logic flaw
Stop testing, since errors mean the application is safely rejecting the request
Pay close attention, because they can disclose details of the back-end behavior that help refine the attack
Report them as the vulnerability without investigating further
questions.explain: Reaching a location in a partly defined or inconsistent state often makes the application complain. Those errors are a valuable source of information disclosure about how the back end works.

questions.q: A shop gives 10% off orders over $1000. An attacker adds items until the cart passes $1000, gets the discount, then removes the unwanted items before placing the order and keeps the discount. What check is missing?
choices: A check that the discount code is spelled correctly
A client-side check that hides the discount banner
A limit on how many items a cart can hold
A check that the order hasn't changed since the discount was applied, so it still meets the criteria when placed
questions.explain: The logic never re-checks the order after the discount is applied. The attacker gets a discount on an order that no longer meets the intended criteria.

questions.q: Which feature of online shops is a classic attack surface when hunting for logic flaws?
choices: Discounting functionality
Product image hosting
Static "About us" pages
The site's CSS stylesheets
questions.explain: Discounting is a potential gold mine, with many basic logic flaws in how discounts get applied.

questions.q: When hunting domain-specific flaws, which situations deserve particular attention?
choices: Pages that only serve static content
Any situation where prices or other sensitive values are adjusted based on criteria determined by user actions
Endpoints that return HTTP 404
Features that require no user input
questions.explain: Work out which algorithms make these adjustments and when they are applied. Then try to put the application in a state where the adjustments no longer match the criteria the developers intended.

questions.q: A tester finds a way to force large numbers of users to follow their social media account but doesn't report it. What best explains how this happens?
choices: Automated scanners already flag every such issue
The behavior can't be reproduced with an intercepting proxy
Without knowledge of the domain, the tester may not see why this is valuable to an attacker and dismisses it
Social media platforms have no business logic
questions.explain: Spotting domain-specific flaws takes an understanding of what an attacker would want in that context. Without it, you may dismiss dangerous behavior or fail to see how two functions combine harmfully.

questions.q: When testing an application from a domain you're unfamiliar with, what is recommended?
choices: Read as much documentation as possible
Where available, talk to subject-matter experts from the domain
Focus on familiar features and skip the domain-specific ones, since they rarely contain bugs
Rely on automated scanners to cover the domain-specific logic
questions.explain: Documentation and subject-matter experts supply the domain knowledge needed to recognize harmful behavior. Domain-specific features are where these flaws live.

questions.q: True or false: The more obscure an application's domain is, the more likely it is that other testers have missed bugs in it.
questions.explain: Learning an obscure domain takes work, but that same difficulty means fewer people have tested it properly.

questions.q: In a web application, what is an "encryption oracle"?
choices: A server that stores all of an application's encryption keys
A user-controllable input that the application encrypts, with the resulting ciphertext then made available to the user in some way
A third-party service that certifies TLS certificates
A brute-force tool for recovering encryption keys
questions.explain: Because the application encrypts attacker-chosen data and returns the ciphertext, the attacker can encrypt arbitrary data with the application's own algorithm and key.

questions.q: When does an encryption oracle become dangerous?
choices: Whenever the application uses TLS
Only when the oracle uses an outdated cipher
When the ciphertext is longer than the plaintext
When other user-controllable inputs expect data encrypted with the same algorithm, so the attacker can produce valid encrypted input for sensitive functions
questions.explain: The attacker uses the oracle to generate valid encrypted data and then passes it into other sensitive functions that trust data encrypted with that algorithm.

questions.q: True or false: To exploit an encryption oracle, the attacker must also find a user-controllable input that performs the matching decryption.
questions.explain: A reverse (decryption) function makes things worse, because the attacker can decrypt data to learn the expected structure. It saves effort but is not necessarily required to build a successful exploit.

questions.q: What mainly determines the severity of an encryption oracle?
choices: The length of the encryption key
How many times the oracle can be called per minute
What other functionality uses the same algorithm as the oracle
Whether the ciphertext is Base64-encoded
questions.explain: The oracle matters only as much as the functions that accept data encrypted with the same algorithm.

questions.q: Some sites parse email addresses to extract the domain and decide which organization the owner belongs to. What causes an email address parser discrepancy?
choices: Different parts of the application handle email addresses differently
The user enters an email address in uppercase
The mail server is temporarily unavailable
The email address contains no domain part
questions.explain: When validation and later processing parse the same address differently, the domain-based logic can be undermined. Email parsing is complex even for valid RFC-compliant addresses.

questions.q: How does an attacker typically exploit an email address parser discrepancy?
choices: By sending a very large number of registration requests
By using encoding techniques to disguise parts of the address, so it passes initial validation but the server's parsing logic interprets it differently
By guessing the administrator's password
By intercepting the confirmation email in transit
questions.explain: Encoding hides parts of the address, so the validation check and the server's parser reach different conclusions about the same address.

questions.q: What is the main impact of email address parser discrepancies?
choices: Denial of service against the mail server
Leaking the plaintext of encrypted emails
Corrupting the application's database
Unauthorized access: registering accounts with seemingly valid addresses from restricted domains to reach areas such as admin panels or restricted user functions
questions.explain: If the application grants privileges based on the email domain, an address that appears to belong to a restricted domain can unlock sensitive functionality.

questions.q: True or false: Extracting the domain from an email address is straightforward as long as the address is valid and RFC-compliant.
questions.explain: It may look simple, but parsing email addresses is very complex even for valid RFC-compliant addresses. That complexity is what leads to parser discrepancies.
